documentation.range: This species is widespread in suitable habitat in sub-Saharan Africa, occurring from as far north as northern Senegal to as far south as northeast South Africa (Spawls et al. 2002), and east as far as Eritrea (Trape and Mané 2006), southern Somalia and Ethiopia (Largen and Rasmussen 1993, Lanza 1990). Based on its distribution in Ethiopia its occurrence in Djibouti is highly likely, but requires confirmation (Ineich 2001). It appears to be absent from Sudan, and has only a marginal occurrence in eastern South Sudan, at Torit (Håkansson and Madsen 1983, Spawls et al. 2002). It occurs in most of East Africa (although few records exist for Burundi - Spawls et al. 2018), and probably occurs throughout Tanzania although records are lacking from much of the country's west (Spawls et al. 2002). It is absent from much of north and central Kenya, from the high plateau between Lake Victoria and Mt. Kenya, and most of Uganda west of Lake Victoria (Spawls et al. 2002). In southern Africa, it is widely distributed in Namibia, Botswana, Zambia and Zimbabwe, being more limited in South Africa to northeastern and coastal eastern parts of the country (Branch 1998, Broadley et al. 2003, Marais 2004, Broadley and Blaylock 2013). In northern West Africa it is known from southern Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, northern Sierra Leone, far northwestern Côte d'Ivoire and southwestern Burkina Faso, where it ranges through all climatic zones south of the Sahel (Trape and Mané 2006). It is apparently absent from Togo (Segniagbeto et al. 2011) and Benin (J. Penner, C. Toudonou and M.-O. Rödel pers. comm. 2012), and records from northern Ghana need to be confirmed. It occurs from sea level to around 1,600 m asl (Spawls et al. 2002), but is not common above 1,000 m (Håkansson and Madsen 1983).
documentation.population: This species is reported to be common (Spawls et al. 2002). In areas with few records this can be attributed to under-collecting rather then low abundance (Spawls et al. 2002).
documentation.habitats: This species is most commonly found in well-wooded savannah or riverine forest, especially in areas with an abundance of rocky hills and big trees. It can also be found in coastal bush, moist and dry savanna and woodland. This species is predominantly found on the ground, however, it is also arboreal (Spawls et al. 2002). An individual may often live more or less permanently in some favoured hole in the ground, hollow log, or rock crevice, from where it will make long excursions in search of food or mates (Largen and Spawls 2010). It will occasionally use the roofs of houses as semi-permanent shelter sites (Spawls et al. 2002). This very fast diurnal snake hunts mainly small mammals, including rodents, insectivores and bats, but will occasionally take birds or snakes (Trape and Mané 2006). Females have been observed to deposit from 6 to 17 eggs (Largen and Spawls 2010). Eggs hatch in 80–90 days (Branch 1998).
documentation.threats: It is unlikely that any major threat is impacting this species across its full range. Black Mambas are shy animals and prefer to avoid human contact. Human population expansion into its habitat could therefore constitute a potential threat to this species. However, the extent of its range throughout much of Africa means that this should not be considered a serious threat.
documentation.measures: There are no known species-specific conservation measures in place for this species, however, in places its distribution coincides with protected areas. No conservation measures are required for this species.
documentation.use_trade: This species is rarely traded. The export quota for Tanzania was 300 animals in 2014. Between 2013 and 2017 51 animals were reported as being advertised for trade across several African states (Tanzania, Guinea, Cameroon and Uganda) by Jensen et al. (2019)
documentation.rationale: This species has been assessed as Least Concern owing to its very large distribution throughout sub-Saharan Africa. No specific threats have been reported and this species is not undergoing significant population declines.
